name: Queen Neferet
epithet: The Lady Who Wants to Go Home

inspiration.oldScript: The orientalist mummy's curse: a foreign dead man menacing the West for revenge.
inspiration.newLens: A queen, taken from her tomb by a collector, who wants to go home. The Best ending is repatriation with dignity.

logline: The Halloween exhibit at the library promises a mummy's curse. What it actually holds is a stolen queen, and she is done waiting to go home.
backstory: Nearly four thousand years ago, Neferet was Great Royal Wife of Egypt, remembered in temple inscriptions for opening the royal granaries in a famine year and for founding a house of healing at Thebes. She was buried on the west bank of the Nile with her name carved on her tomb and her coffin, so that it would be spoken and she would live on. In 1911 an American railroad heir named Cornelius Halvorsen paid men to dig at night, bribed the inspector who tried to stop him, and shipped the queen to Minneapolis in a crate stenciled MACHINE PARTS. For seventy-five years the Halvorsen Foundation has toured her as THE MUMMY'S CURSE!, beneath a placard calling her an unknown noblewoman. In 1972 Egypt's Antiquities Organization formally asked for her return. The Foundation never answered. This October the tour stops at the Glimmer Falls Public Library, a few blocks from the Heartstone, and the geode has woken her. She does not want revenge. She wants her name back, and she wants to go home. But a queen who has waited seventy-five years can be frightening in her patience: sand pours from the library's book drop, the sky over Crystal Street turns into the stars of another country, and anyone who handles the exhibit starts to forget their own name.

centralIssue.title: Theft of heritage
centralIssue.summary: Queen Neferet was never cursed. She was stolen, relabeled "unknown" and sold as a sideshow while her own country asked for her back. Destroying her, or nailing her back in a crate, only repeats the theft. Restore her name and help her go home with dignity.

poster: A regal ancient Egyptian queen in white linen and a gold vulture crown standing calm and luminous above a small-town public library at night, an immense starry figure of a sky goddess arching over the suburban rooftops, golden sand pouring softly from the library's book-return slot, a teenage crew looking up from the steps
portrait: Close portrait of a dignified ancient Egyptian queen with dark kohl-lined eyes, a gold and lapis broad collar and a vulture crown, her expression patient and sorrowful, lit by the warm glow of a museum case lamp, faint stars moving behind her
endingPhoto: A regal ancient Egyptian queen in white linen and a gold vulture crown standing calm and luminous in the reading room of a small-town library at night, golden sand pouring from the card catalog drawers, an immense starry sky goddess arching across the ceiling, teens peering over a stack of encyclopedias holding a library card like a talisman
taunts: Say my name. It is a small thing. Surely you can manage a small thing.
You put a card on my bed that says unknown. I know exactly who I am.
I have waited seventy-five years in boxes. I can wait one more night in your dreams.
Everything taken wants to go home, child. Look in your own drawers.

clues.title: Her name
clues.hint: The traveling exhibit in the library's museum room has a placard that gets one very important thing wrong.

encounter.title: Unknown Noblewoman
encounter.place: The traveling exhibit room, Glimmer Falls Public Library
encounter.text: The Halvorsen exhibit fills the library's museum room with fake torches, plastic palm fronds and a looping cassette of thunder. A banner promises THE MUMMY'S CURSE! ENTER IF YOU DARE! In the center case lies a painted coffin with a calm golden face, and the typed placard reads only: MUMMY OF AN UNKNOWN NOBLEWOMAN, PROVENANCE PRIVATE. But on the lid, inside a carved oval, are hieroglyphs nobody here has bothered to read.
encounter.art: A small-town library museum room cluttered with plastic palm fronds and fake tiki torches, a cheap cloth drape painted with pyramids hanging crooked on the wall, and in the center a glass case holding an ancient painted wooden coffin with a calm golden face, a carved oval on its lid filled with tiny painted birds, eyes and reeds, a 16-year-old Indian American girl with a long braid and round gold glasses and a teenager bent over a thick reference book beside the case, warm display lights, medium wide shot

choices.label: Sit down with Priya and a hieroglyph dictionary and read the oval yourselves

success.text: It takes an hour, three reference books and a lot of Priya muttering. The oval is a cartouche, the frame around a royal name. The heart-and-windpipe sign for nefer, beautiful. A bread loaf for the t. A seated woman. "Neferet," Priya breathes. "And that title before it means Great Royal Wife. She isn't unknown. She's a queen." The thunder tape clicks off by itself.
success.alone: It takes an hour, three reference books and a lot of muttering under your breath. The oval is a cartouche, the frame around a royal name. The heart-and-windpipe sign for nefer, beautiful. A bread loaf for the t. A seated woman. "Neferet," you breathe. And that title before it means Great Royal Wife. She isn't unknown. She's a queen. The thunder tape clicks off by itself.
success.art: Two teenagers hunched over reference books and notebooks beside a glass exhibit case, one pointing at a carved cartouche on a painted coffin lid, sketches of hieroglyphs spread across the floor

failure.text: The glyphs swim. Your library book falls open to a lurid chapter about curses written in 1950 by a man who never left Ohio, and the fake torches gutter like real ones. When you look up, the placard reads UNKNOWN in bigger letters than before, and for one horrible second, so does the name patch on your jacket.
failure.art: A teenager in a dim exhibit room staring at a placard reading unknown in large letters, the same word appearing on the name patch of their jacket, fake torches flickering

choices.label: Ask Ms. Hart about the exhibit's loan contract

success.text: Ms. Hart pulls the contract from a folder with visible distaste. "I asked them for a real Egyptologist's notes. They sent a press kit with a cartoon skeleton on it." Stapled to the back is a 1958 conservator's report the Foundation forgot to remove: Cartouche reads NEFERET, Great Royal Wife. Recommend correcting placard. Nobody ever did.
success.art: A librarian in a cardigan at her desk holding up a stapled contract with a typed conservator's report attached, a glossy cartoon skeleton press kit tossed aside

failure.text: Ms. Hart is on the phone with the Foundation's touring manager, who is shouting about ticket sales. She mouths "later." On your way out, the coffin's painted eyes follow you to the door, patient and unblinking, and the air smells like cedar and hot sand.
failure.art: A painted coffin face in a glass case whose eyes seem to follow a teenager leaving the room, a librarian on a phone in the background, a thin drift of sand on the floor

clues.title: The 1911 diary
clues.hint: The exhibit's souvenir kiosk in the Starlight Mall food court is run by the last of the Halvorsens.

encounter.title: Pharaoh Phun
encounter.text: Between the pretzel stand and Orange Jubilee, a kiosk called PHARAOH PHUN sells plaster scarabs, glow-in-the-dark mummy keychains and T-shirts that say I SURVIVED THE CURSE. Behind the register slumps Gil Halvorsen, thirty-something, great-grandson of the collector, in a pith helmet he clearly hates. Under the counter, propping up the cash drawer, is a cracked leather journal stamped C.H. 1911.
encounter.art: A tacky mall food court kiosk under pink neon, shelves of plaster scarabs, glow-in-the-dark cartoon mummy keychains and folded T-shirts, a tired man in his thirties slumped at the register in a khaki pith helmet, a cracked old leather journal wedged under the cash drawer, a wiry teenage boy with a lightning bolt shaved into his hair waving him toward an arcade machine, a teenager at the counter, neon and fluorescent light, medium shot

choices.label: Buy a keychain and ask Gil about his great-grandfather

success.text: Gil laughs, not happily. "You want to know the real curse? It's this kiosk." He slides the journal across the counter. Cornelius wrote it all down: the night dig, the local men who begged him to stop, the bribe, the crate stenciled MACHINE PARTS. "I read it when I was twelve," Gil says. "I've been selling plastic beetles about it ever since. I'm so tired."
success.art: A weary man in a pith helmet sliding an old leather journal across a kiosk counter to a teenager holding a plastic keychain, food court neon all around

failure.text: Gil gives you the tourist speech, the one about eerie happenings at every tour stop, and he gives it like a man reading his own ransom note. When you ask about the journal he says "What journal?" and lays his hand flat on the counter. Every plaster scarab on the shelf turns to face the library.
failure.art: Rows of plaster scarabs on a kiosk shelf all turned in the same direction, a man in a pith helmet pressing his hand flat on a counter, a teenager looking uneasy

choices.label: Have Lou distract Gil while you slide the journal out

success.text: Lou challenges Gil to one game of Galaxia for a free T-shirt, and Gil, who is very bored, accepts. Behind the pretzel stand you read: "The village men are angry. They say she is their queen and their ancestor. I paid the inspector double." You photocopy six pages at the drugstore and slip the journal back before Gil loses his last life.
success.art: A teenager reading an old leather journal behind a pretzel stand while in the background an arcade kid and a man in a pith helmet play a glowing cabinet game

failure.text: The cash drawer pops open with a ding when you tug the journal free. Mall security walks you to the exit and bans you from the food court for the day. Through the glass doors you see Gil reading the journal himself, his face in his hands.
failure.art: A teenager being escorted out of a mall by a security guard, through the glass doors a man in a pith helmet sitting at a kiosk with his face in his hands over an open journal

clues.title: The 1972 request
clues.hint: Mrs. Mansour on Crystal Street taught history in Luxor for thirty years before she moved here to be near her grandchildren.

encounter.title: Tea on the Porch
encounter.text: Mrs. Hoda Mansour's porch is the only one on Crystal Street with a lemon tree in a pot and a glass of mint tea waiting for whoever comes by. She saw the exhibit poster at the grocery store and has not stopped frowning since. "The mummy's curse," she says, setting down her crossword. "Seventy-five years, and still they have not learned her name. Sit. Have you eaten?"
encounter.art: A sunny suburban porch with a potted lemon tree, an Egyptian American woman in her sixties with silver-streaked dark hair, reading glasses and a soft cardigan setting down a newspaper crossword, glasses of mint tea and a plate of date cookies on a little table, a teenager sitting on the porch steps holding a pencil sketch, warm afternoon sun, medium shot

choices.label: Sit down, eat the date cookies and listen

success.text: She tells you about Neferet the way you'd talk about a famous great-aunt: the famine year, the open granaries, the house of healing. Then she brings out a carbon copy from a shoebox. "My brother typed this in 1972, at the Antiquities Organization in Cairo. A formal request for her return. They never even wrote back." She presses it into your hands. "Maybe they will listen to children."
success.art: An older woman on a porch handing a faded carbon-copy letter to a teenager, a shoebox of papers and photographs open between them, a lemon tree and tea glasses in afternoon light

failure.text: She asks why you want to know, and you mumble something about the curse because you're nervous, and her face closes like a door. "There is no curse," she says quietly. "There is only a theft." She goes inside. The lemon tree drops a single lemon onto the step, and it rolls downhill toward the library.
failure.art: A closed front door on a quiet porch, a single lemon rolling down the steps and along the sidewalk, a teenager left alone with an untouched glass of tea

choices.label: Show her a sketch of the coffin's carving and ask what it means to her

success.text: She reads it before you finish holding it up. "Neferet. Great Royal Wife." Her eyes fill. "On the west bank where I grew up, the old women still say her name at the harvest. We never stopped." From a drawer she takes her brother's 1972 letter to the Halvorsen Foundation, still sealed in the envelope it came back in, stamped by the Foundation's lawyers: RETURN TO SENDER.
success.art: An older woman with tears in her eyes holding up a sketch of a cartouche on her porch, a teenager beside her, an old unopened envelope stamped return to sender laid on the table

failure.text: Your sketch is smudged and upside down, and Mrs. Mansour has to turn it the right way with a patient sigh. Before she can read it, the sky over Crystal Street dims in the middle of the afternoon, and a cold wind smelling of river mud tears the paper from your hand and down a storm drain.
failure.art: A sheet of paper whirling away down a suburban storm drain in a sudden dim wind, an older woman and a teenager on a porch shielding their eyes, the afternoon sky darkening

signature.title: The Night Drop
signature.place: The book-return slot, Glimmer Falls Public Library, midnight
signature.text: You are returning an overdue paperback at midnight when the library's brass book-return slot breathes out warm air that smells of cedar and river mud. Fine golden sand trickles out over your sneakers. A woman's voice, low and very old and perfectly polite, speaks from inside the slot in a language you don't know, then tries again in English: "What is your name? Tell me yours, and I will tell you mine."
signature.art: A brass library book-return slot in a stone wall at midnight, fine golden sand trickling out of it over a teenager's sneakers, a warm amber glow inside the slot, an overdue paperback in the teen's hand, the dark library building above and a single streetlight, close medium shot from low

choices.label: Tell her your real name

success.text: You say your name into the slot. There is a long pause, then a sound like a smile. "Thank you. It has been so long since anyone gave me their name freely." The sand stops. On the step lies a tiny blue faience bead, cool and smooth, and holding it makes you feel braver.
success.art: A teenager kneeling to speak into a glowing library book slot at night, a tiny blue faience bead resting on the stone step before them

failure.text: Your voice catches and your name comes out wrong, half a name. The slot sighs. For the rest of the night you keep almost forgetting what to call yourself, and before morning you have to read it off your library card twice.
failure.art: A teenager in bed at night squinting at their own library card by flashlight, a faint drift of golden sand on the blanket

choices.label: Give her a fake name, just to be safe

success.text: "Rambo," you say. The voice pauses, then laughs, warm and startled, like a queen at a clever jester. "A name of war. Very well, small warrior. Keep your true one safe. I understand that better than anyone." The sand blows back into the slot and the brass flap clicks shut.
success.art: Golden sand swirling back up into a library book slot at night, a teenager grinning nervously on the steps, a faint glow fading behind the brass flap

failure.text: "That is not your name," she says, and suddenly she sounds every one of her four thousand years. "I know what it is to be called by the wrong name." Sand pours from the slot in a rushing golden wave that buries you to the knees, and you dig yourself out with your library card.
failure.art: A golden wave of sand pouring from a library book slot burying a teenager to the knees on the front steps at night

signature.title: Another Sky
signature.text: You look up and the sky is wrong. The Big Dipper is gone. Instead an immense figure made of stars arches over Crystal Street from horizon to horizon, a woman's body bent like a bridge, and beneath her shine the stars of a sky four thousand years and eight thousand miles away. Down the street, the names are lifting off the mailboxes, letter by letter, and drifting upward like sparks.
signature.art: A suburban cul-de-sac at three in the morning beneath an enormous figure of a woman made of stars arching across the entire sky from horizon to horizon, bent in a high arch, strange tilted constellations under her, small glowing metal shapes lifting off the mailboxes and drifting upward as sparks, a teenager in pajamas on a lawn staring up, a skinny boy in a backwards red cap chasing the sparks, deep blue starlight, wide shot

choices.label: Chase the floating letters and stick them back on the mailboxes

success.text: You and Kev sprint down the street plucking glowing letters out of the air. Kev knows every mailbox by heart: that D belongs to the Dobbses, that loose O is the Oyelaran twins. By four a.m. every name is back, slightly crooked, and the starry woman overhead seems to nod.
success.alone: You sprint down the street plucking glowing letters out of the air, checking every mailbox by flashlight: that D belongs to the Dobbses, that loose O is the Oyelaran twins. By four a.m. every name is back, slightly crooked, and the starry woman overhead seems to nod.
success.art: A teenager and a young paperboy leaping to catch glowing letters out of the night air and pressing them onto suburban mailboxes under a starry sky figure

failure.text: The letters slip through your fingers like hot sparks. By dawn three mailboxes are blank, and the families inside wake up confused, calling each other "hey, you" over breakfast, unable to remember what to call their own dog.
failure.art: Three blank mailboxes on a suburban street at dawn, a confused family at a kitchen table visible through a window, a puzzled dog with a blank name tag

choices.label: Lie down on the lawn and try to understand this sky

success.text: Bea brings her star chart and you both lie in the wet grass, comparing. "That's Orion," she says, "but tilted, like from way farther south." The arching woman's starry hand points one way, steady as a compass needle: east, across the ocean. She is not attacking. She is showing you where home is.
success.alone: You dig out your old star chart and lie in the wet grass, comparing. That's Orion, but tilted, like from way farther south. The arching woman's starry hand points one way, steady as a compass needle: east, across the ocean. She is not attacking. She is showing you where home is.
success.art: A teenager and a small girl with a star chart lying on a dewy suburban lawn at night, pointing up at a giant starry woman arching overhead whose hand points toward the horizon

failure.text: You stare too long. The stars rush closer, and for a dizzy moment you are very small and very far away, lying in a sealed wooden crate in the dark hold of a ship, with no idea where you are going or why. You wake on the lawn crying, sand in your hair.
failure.art: A dreamlike vision of a sealed wooden crate stenciled machine parts in the dark hold of an old steamship, overlaid with a teenager curled up on a dewy lawn

signature.title: Machine Parts
signature.text: The Halvorsen Foundation's truck is backed up to the library loading dock, and in the back, under a moving blanket, sits the original 1911 shipping crate, stenciled MACHINE PARTS. Mr. Ferreira, the night custodian, won't go near it. "It knocks," he tells you, and crosses himself. As if on cue, from inside the crate come three slow, polite knocks, the way a guest knocks when she has been kept waiting at the door for a very long time.
signature.art: A library loading dock at eleven at night under a buzzing caged bulb, a battered old wooden shipping crate with faded stenciled paint in the back of a box truck under a gray moving blanket, a middle-aged custodian in coveralls clutching a mop and backing away, a teenager stepping closer with a raised fist ready to knock, golden sand trickling from a seam in the crate, yellow bulb light, medium wide shot

choices.label: Knock back three times and ask who is there

success.text: You knock three times. A pause, then a voice through the slats, dry as papyrus and perfectly gracious: "Someone with manners. At last." She asks you to read her the stencil on the crate, and you do. "Machine parts," she repeats, and the silence that follows is worse than any scream. "That is what they called me. Remember it."
success.art: A teenager kneeling with one ear against a weathered wooden crate in the back of a truck, knuckles raised to knock, a thin stream of golden sand glittering out between the slats

failure.text: You knock. The crate knocks back, faster. Then every crate, box and filing cabinet on the loading dock starts knocking, hundreds of knocks at once, until Mr. Ferreira drops his mop and runs, and you run right behind him.
failure.art: A custodian and a teenager fleeing a library loading dock at night while stacked crates and filing cabinets rattle and shake, dust and golden sand puffing from every seam

choices.label: Find a crowbar and pry the lid off

success.text: The nails shriek out one by one. Inside there is no monster, only old straw and the small things that were packed around her and then forgotten: a pair of reed sandals, a wooden boat the size of your hand, a jar sealed with wax. Little things for a long journey. You suddenly feel like a burglar, and you set the lid back very gently.
success.art: An opened wooden crate full of old straw holding small ancient objects, reed sandals, a tiny carved wooden boat and a wax-sealed jar, a teenager holding a crowbar and looking ashamed under a caged bulb

failure.text: The lid springs up on its own and a blast of hot desert wind knocks you flat. Sand pours out, ankle-deep, then knee-deep, and by the time you dig yourself free, the loading dock is a dune and Mr. Ferreira is on the pay phone, calling his priest.
failure.art: A teenager half buried in a drift of golden sand on a library loading dock at night, a wooden crate lid hanging open in the truck above, a custodian at a pay phone in the background

choices.label: Ask Delphine to dig out the exhibit's shipping papers

success.text: Delphine finds the folder in about four minutes, because she is Delphine. The 1911 bill of lading lists one crate, Alexandria to Minneapolis, MACHINE PARTS, customs inspection waived, signed with a flourish by C. Halvorsen. Delphine's mouth goes thin. "That," she says, "is a confession on letterhead."
success.alone: You find the folder after twenty dusty minutes in the library office's filing cabinet. The 1911 bill of lading lists one crate, Alexandria to Minneapolis, MACHINE PARTS, customs inspection waived, signed with a flourish by C. Halvorsen. Your mouth goes thin. That is a confession on letterhead.
success.art: A librarian in a cardigan and a teenager bent over a yellowed shipping document under a green desk lamp in a cluttered library office, an old red wax customs seal on the page

failure.text: The exhibit's paperwork is a single page: PROPERTY OF THE HALVORSEN FOUNDATION, PROVENANCE PRIVATE. While you're reading it, the lights dim, the office fills with the smell of cedar and river mud, and the filing cabinet drawers slide open one by one, all on their own.
failure.art: A dim library office with filing cabinet drawers sliding open one by one, a librarian and a teenager staring in alarm, faint golden dust drifting through the lamplight

signature.title: That Is Not How It Happened
signature.place: The Glitter Box Playhouse, midnight double feature
signature.text: Frankie Fontaine has booked the 1932 mummy picture for the Glitter Box midnight show, and the crowd is having a ball, booing the villain and tossing popcorn. Then the movie stops. On the screen, the bandaged figure turns, looks straight out at the audience and unwinds its wrappings, and underneath is a woman in white linen and gold. She steps out of the light onto the stage, and the theater goes silent. "That," says Queen Neferet, "is not how it happened."
signature.art: A plush old community theater at midnight, a projector beam cutting through haze, a regal ancient Egyptian queen with kohl-lined eyes, a white linen gown, a gold and lapis broad collar and a gold vulture crown stepping off the glowing movie screen onto the stage with loose white bandages falling at her feet, the audience frozen mid popcorn toss, a teenager standing in the aisle, silver projector light, wide shot

choices.label: Ask her to tell it the way it really happened

success.text: Frankie kills the reel and brings the house lights up halfway. Neferet stands in the projector beam and tells it: the famine year, the granaries she opened, the house of healing at Thebes, the night men came with shovels. Nobody throws popcorn. When she finishes, someone in the balcony starts to clap, then the whole room does, and the queen inclines her head.
success.alone: You sprint up to the booth, kill the reel and bring the house lights up halfway. Neferet stands in the projector beam and tells it: the famine year, the granaries she opened, the house of healing at Thebes, the night men came with shovels. Nobody throws popcorn. When she finishes, someone in the balcony starts to clap, then the whole room does, and the queen inclines her head.
success.art: A queen in white linen and gold standing in a projector beam on a theater stage speaking with dignity, an audience in red velvet seats rising to applaud, a stage manager in a headset at the side of the stage

failure.text: You ask, but the crowd won't hush. Somebody yells "Boo!" out of pure habit. The queen's eyes go dark as a tomb, and sand begins to rise over the seats while the projector shows the same scene of a crate being nailed shut, over and over.
failure.art: Golden sand rising over red velvet theater seats while patrons scramble, a movie screen showing a wooden crate being nailed shut, a stern queen in white and gold on the stage

choices.label: Turn on the movie with Glory and roast its curse nonsense

success.text: You and Glory turn on the film instead. "A curse? Honey, she was ROBBED!" Glory booms as the reel starts again. You narrate every scene the way it actually went, and the audience joins in. Up on stage, Neferet laughs for the first time in four thousand years, a sound like wind chimes in a dry wind.
success.alone: You turn on the film instead. "A curse? Come on, she was ROBBED!" you boom as the reel starts again. You narrate every scene the way it actually went, and the audience joins in. Up on stage, Neferet laughs for the first time in four thousand years, a sound like wind chimes in a dry wind.
success.art: A drag queen in sequins and a teenager standing on their seats shouting at a movie screen in a crowded theater, the audience laughing along, a queen in white linen and gold laughing on the stage

failure.text: The crowd thinks you're heckling her. The queen turns, slowly, and looks at you, and you learn what four thousand years of disappointment feels like aimed at one person. You sit down. You stay down until the house lights come up at three.
failure.art: A teenager sinking low into a red velvet theater seat under the cold gaze of a regal queen in white and gold on the stage, a drag queen beside them wincing

choices.label: Climb to the booth and splice in a different ending

success.text: Toby holds the flashlight while you razor out the scene where the heroes burn her scroll and tape in the travelogue short from the other can: the Nile at sunset, boats on the water, the west bank. Home. When the projector rolls again, the queen on stage watches it with her hand over her heart.
success.alone: With the flashlight clamped in your teeth, you razor out the scene where the heroes burn her scroll and tape in the travelogue short from the other can: the Nile at sunset, boats on the water, the west bank. Home. When the projector rolls again, the queen on stage watches it with her hand over her heart.
success.art: A teenager and a boy with a flashlight splicing a strip of film in a cramped projection booth, through the booth window a screen glows with the Nile at sunset, a queen on stage with a hand over her heart

failure.text: The film snaps, whips off the reel and wraps you up from ankles to chin like, well, a mummy. You hop out of the booth to cheers from an audience who thinks it's part of the show, and a queen who very clearly does not find it funny.
failure.art: A teenager wrapped head to toe in shiny loops of movie film hopping out of a projection booth doorway, a cheering theater crowd below, a queen on stage with arms folded

signature.title: Everything Walks Home
signature.text: A soft scraping sound wakes you. Out on Crystal Street, things are walking home. A stolen stop sign is hopping back to the corner of Vista Way. The Lindgrens' garden gnome, swiped in 1979, is trudging up their driveway trailing golden sand. A library book eleven years overdue flaps past like a tired bird. A cool, patient voice says, "Everything taken wants to go home." And in your own dresser drawer, something is knocking to be let out.
signature.art: A moonlit suburban street at two in the morning, a stolen stop-shaped red metal plate on a post hopping back to a street corner, a garden gnome trudging up a driveway trailing golden sand, an old library book flapping through the air, plastic flamingos waddling home, a teenager watching wide-eyed from a bedroom window with a dresser drawer rattling behind them, white moonlight, wide shot

choices.label: Open the drawer and walk your own borrowed thing home

success.text: It's your neighbor Leticia's tape player, borrowed in June and never returned. You pull on a jacket and walk it three blocks to her porch, where it settles on the mat with a contented click. When you turn around, the stars overhead have shifted, just slightly, and a voice that sounds almost pleased says, "So you do understand."
success.art: A teenager in a jacket setting a portable cassette player gently on a front porch mat at night, golden sand glittering in a trail behind them, a strange sky of unfamiliar stars overhead

failure.text: You open the drawer and the tape player bolts. You chase it six blocks in your pajamas, past porch after porch of neighbors watching their own lost things leave, and you finally corner it at the Heartstone roundabout, where it nips your finger and escapes into the dark.
failure.art: A teenager in pajamas sprinting down a moonlit street after a small portable cassette player scuttling away on a trail of golden sand, neighbors in doorways watching, a giant purple geode ahead

choices.label: Follow the trails of sand to see where they all lead

success.text: Kev knows every house on his route, so he knows which trails don't belong to it. Every stolen thing on Crystal Street finds its own way home, but the sand they shed all drifts, sooner or later, the same direction: toward the library, where one window in the exhibit room glows gold. She's showing you what going home looks like.
success.alone: You know every house on Crystal Street, so you know which trails don't belong to it. Every stolen thing on Crystal Street finds its own way home, but the sand they shed all drifts, sooner or later, the same direction: toward the library, where one window in the exhibit room glows gold. She's showing you what going home looks like.
success.art: A teenager and a young paperboy with a canvas bag following glittering trails of golden sand down a dark street toward a distant library with one window glowing gold, little lost objects marching ahead

failure.text: The trails cross and recross until you're walking in circles on a sidewalk you've walked a thousand times, and the house numbers have all changed. You wake at dawn curled on a stranger's porch swing with sand in your sneakers and no idea how you got there.
failure.art: A teenager asleep curled on a porch swing at dawn with sand spilling from their sneakers, looping glittering trails of sand crisscrossing the sidewalk below in tangled spirals

choices.label: Grab a pillowcase and stuff the escaping things inside

success.text: You bag a gnome, two plastic flamingos and a runaway bowling trophy and tie the pillowcase shut. It thrashes, then goes still, then very politely knocks. You sit with it on the curb until you feel bad enough to let them out, and they hurry off without a backward glance. You did learn something, mostly about yourself.
success.art: A teenager sitting on a curb at night beside a lumpy pillowcase, a garden gnome and two plastic lawn flamingos hurrying away down the moonlit street, golden sand glittering in their wake

failure.text: The pillowcase gets heavier with every stolen thing you stuff in, then heavier on its own, until you can't lift it, and then it starts dragging you down the street toward the library, very patiently, the way a river drags a stick.
failure.art: A teenager clinging to a bulging pillowcase that drags them along a moonlit suburban street toward a distant library glowing gold, golden sand streaming behind

signature.title: The Hall of Glass Cases
signature.place: The exhibit room, endlessly, in a dream
signature.text: You fall asleep at the kitchen table and wake up in the exhibit room, except now it goes on forever: case after glass case under humming lights, and in every case lies someone from Glimmer Falls, eyes closed, hands folded. Your neighbors. Your crew. Every placard reads UNKNOWN, PROVENANCE PRIVATE. At the far end, a tall woman in white linen and a gold crown stands with her back to you. "Now you know," she says, "how it feels."
signature.art: An endless museum hall of glass display cases under humming lights, each case holding a sleeping neighbor or teenager with eyes closed and hands folded, a small typed placard at the foot of each, a teenager in pajamas standing among the cases, and at the far end a tall Egyptian queen in white linen and a gold vulture crown standing with her back turned, cold white case light, long wide shot

choices.label: Grab a marker and write everyone's real names on the placards

success.text: You uncap a marker and go case to case: Pearl Washington. Bea Lindqvist. Mr. Dobbs from down the street, Howard, it turns out. Each time you write a name, the person inside opens their eyes and sits up. When you turn around, the queen is watching you, and her face is no longer carved stone. "Yes," she says. "Like that. Do it for me."
success.art: A teenager writing names on museum placards with a marker as sleeping neighbors sit up inside their glass cases, a queen in white linen and gold watching with softened eyes

failure.text: The marker is dry. Then it is full of sand. You scrape at the placards with your fingernails until a guard in a pith helmet, with no face beneath it, takes your elbow very gently and leads you toward an empty case with your height written on the side.
failure.art: A faceless guard in a pith helmet gently leading a teenager by the elbow toward an empty glass display case, sand spilling from a broken marker

choices.label: Smash the nearest case and drag your friend out

success.text: Glass rains down and your friend gasps awake in your arms. An alarm wails and the whole endless hall shivers. The queen turns her head. "You would break a case to bring someone home," she says. "Then you understand everything. Why does no one break mine?" You wake gripping your friend's hand across the kitchen table.
success.art: A teenager pulling a friend out of a shattered display case in a dreamlike museum hall, glass shards glittering in the air, a crowned queen turning to look

failure.text: The glass is as thick as a bank vault. Your knuckles thud uselessly and your friend sleeps on, placard and all. The lights dim one row at a time, closing in on you, and you wake on the kitchen floor at dawn with your name traced in sand on the linoleum, misspelled.
failure.art: A teenager pounding bruised fists on thick display glass as rows of museum lights go dark behind them, a friend sleeping peacefully inside the case

signature.title: Read the Curse Out Loud!
signature.place: A sleepover in the Oyelarans' basement, midnight
signature.text: Somebody brought a souvenir from the library exhibit's gift kiosk: a rolled parchment scroll, $1.99, printed in Minneapolis, with READ THE MUMMY'S CURSE OUT LOUD! IF YOU DARE! across the top. Everyone at the sleepover takes a turn hamming it up, flashlight under the chin. On the fourth turn every flashlight dims to candle glow, fine golden sand hisses out of the heating vent, and a woman's voice, low and very old and deeply unimpressed, speaks from the dark: "That is not my language. That is nonsense your grandfather's printer invented." The fake squiggles on the scroll begin to crawl.
signature.art: A cozy 1980s basement sleepover at midnight, teenagers in sleeping bags with flashlights dimmed to a warm amber glow, a cheap souvenir parchment scroll unrolled on the shag carpet with black squiggly ink marks crawling off the paper, fine golden sand hissing out of a heating vent in the paneled wall, one teen standing on the couch, amber light and dark corners, wide shot

choices.label: Roll up the scroll and apologize to her, sincerely

success.text: You roll up the scroll and say to the dark, "Sorry. We didn't know. It's a gift-shop thing." A long pause, and then, a little gentler: "I know what it is. Seventy-five years of children shrieking my so-called curse at each other, and you are the first to say sorry." The sand stops and the flashlights come back up. On the carpet the squiggles have gathered into one neat oval, a name inside a ring, that none of you can read yet.
success.art: A teenager kneeling on a basement carpet rolling up a souvenir scroll with an apologetic face, sleepover friends sitting up in sleeping bags, flashlights brightening, a small glowing oval of golden sand on the carpet

failure.text: You try to apologize, and out of habit it comes out in the spooky curse voice. Sand pours from every vent in the basement, ankle-deep and warm as a beach at noon, and everyone spends the rest of the night on the couch.
failure.art: Teens huddled together on a basement couch with flashlights, warm golden sand pooled ankle deep across the carpet, sleeping bags half buried, a heating vent pouring more

choices.label: Have Priya study the scroll and prove the curse is a fake

success.text: Priya holds the scroll under a flashlight for ten seconds. "These aren't hieroglyphs. It's the English alphabet in a spooky font. Look, A, B, C." She decodes it out loud, and the ancient curse reads THANK YOU FOR VISITING THE HALVORSEN COLLECTION. The voice in the dark laughs, low and delighted. "A scholar. Finally."
success.alone: You hold the scroll under a flashlight for ten seconds. These aren't hieroglyphs. It's the English alphabet in a spooky font: look, A, B, C. You decode it out loud, and the ancient curse reads THANK YOU FOR VISITING THE HALVORSEN COLLECTION. The voice in the dark laughs, low and delighted. "A scholar. Finally."
success.art: A teen girl with glasses studying a souvenir parchment scroll under a flashlight and pointing at its squiggles, friends leaning in amazed, golden sand settling quietly around a heating vent

failure.text: Priya starts to decode it, and the squiggles crawl off the paper and up her arm like ants. She flings the scroll across the basement into the popcorn bowl. Nobody touches the popcorn again.
failure.alone: You start to decode it, and the squiggles crawl off the paper and up your arm like ants. You fling the scroll across the basement into the popcorn bowl. Nobody touches the popcorn again.
failure.art: Spooky ink squiggles crawling off a souvenir scroll like a line of ants, teens shrieking and leaping out of sleeping bags, a bowl of popcorn spilling, amber flashlight glow

choices.label: Grab the scroll and read the curse even louder

success.text: You stand on the couch and bellow the whole fake curse at the top of your lungs, and of course it does absolutely zilch. The voice in the dark sighs. "Yes. Exactly. It does nothing. It never did. There was never a curse, child. There was a robbery." The sand stops, and the whole sleepover stares at you, and then at the vent.
success.art: A teenager standing on a basement couch bellowing from a souvenir scroll, sleepover friends staring wide-eyed, golden sand settling around a heating vent, flashlights glowing amber

failure.text: "Since you enjoy it so much," the voice says coolly, and you can't stop. You read the gift-shop curse forty-one times in a row, in a spooky voice, while your friends fall asleep one by one around you.
failure.art: A hoarse exhausted teenager reading from a souvenir scroll at dawn, sleepover friends asleep in sleeping bags around them, pale light through a small basement window, drifts of golden sand

signature.title: Live at Eleven: Breaking the Curse
signature.place: The library exhibit room, live on Channel 8, 11 p.m.
signature.text: The Halvorsen Foundation has hired Madame Zorova, Psychic to the Stars, to break the Mummy's Curse live on Channel 8's late news, and half of Glimmer Falls is crowded outside the library windows with flashlights to watch. Madame Zorova waves a smoking bundle of incense over the coffin and announces she will release the evil spirit by burning the queen's linen wrappings. A Foundation man in a blazer is already holding the lighter. The coffin trembles, sand lifts off the floor in slow spinning ribbons, and the voice you know from the book drop says, very quietly, "Again?"
signature.art: A library exhibit room under harsh television news lights at eleven at night, a flamboyant fake psychic in a sequined purple cape and turban waving a smoking bundle of incense over an ancient painted coffin, a man in a blazer holding a lit lighter, a news camera on a tripod, ribbons of golden sand rising off the floor in slow spirals, townspeople pressed against the windows with flashlights, a teenager stepping in front of the coffin, white TV light, wide shot

choices.label: Step between the lighter and the coffin

success.text: You step in front of the coffin with the TV lights in your eyes. "Nobody's burning anything. She's a person. She's a queen." The camera swings to your face, and across Glimmer Falls a few thousand people watch a teenager refuse to move until the Foundation man lowers the lighter. Behind you the sand settles to the floor, every grain, like a held breath let go.
success.art: A teenager standing with arms spread before an ancient painted coffin, squinting into television lights, a man in a blazer lowering a lighter, a camera operator filming, golden sand settling to the floor

failure.text: Two rent-a-cops walk you out past the camera while Madame Zorova intones, "You see? The curse has possessed the young." It runs on the late news, and your mom sees it.
failure.art: Two security guards escorting a teenager past a television camera outside a library at night, a sequined fake psychic gesturing dramatically, a crowd with flashlights watching

choices.label: Take the news mic and tell the town what she really is

success.text: You take the microphone right out of the anchorman's hand. "There's no curse," you tell Glimmer Falls. "There's a woman somebody dug up and shipped here in a crate marked machine parts. She has a name. She wants to go home." Outside the windows the flashlights lower one by one, and the anchorman doesn't ask for his mic back. Somewhere in the room a very old voice says, "Again. Louder."
success.art: A teenager speaking earnestly into a news microphone under bright television lights, a startled anchorman beside them, townspeople outside the library windows lowering their flashlights, an ancient painted coffin behind

failure.text: The anchorman yanks the mic back and cuts to commercial while Madame Zorova laughs. The sand rises to your knees, and outside the windows people scream and run, which is exactly the story Channel 8 wanted.
failure.art: Golden sand swirling knee deep in a library exhibit room, an anchorman clutching his microphone, a sequined psychic laughing, townspeople fleeing from the windows into the night

choices.label: Out-psychic the psychic, live on camera

success.text: Raven shuffles a real tarot deck, cool as ice, and you announce on live TV that you're reading Madame Zorova's future. "I see a lawsuit. I see a refund. I see you getting in your car, right now." Raven flips the Tower for emphasis. Madame Zorova looks at the trembling coffin, then at Raven, grabs her incense and leaves, and from the coffin comes a sound suspiciously like a laugh.
success.alone: You shuffle a real tarot deck, cool as ice, and announce on live TV that you're reading Madame Zorova's future. "I see a lawsuit. I see a refund. I see you getting in your car, right now." You flip the Tower for emphasis. Madame Zorova looks at the trembling coffin, then at you, grabs her incense and leaves, and from the coffin comes a sound suspiciously like a laugh.
success.art: A goth teen in thrifted velvet flipping a tarot card with deadpan confidence beside a teenager pointing dramatically, a sequined fake psychic fleeing with smoking incense, television lights, an ancient coffin behind

failure.text: Madame Zorova reads YOUR future first, very loudly, on live TV, and it involves a great deal of detention. The audience at home laughs at you, and the man with the lighter steps closer to the coffin.
failure.art: A sequined fake psychic pointing dramatically at a mortified teenager under television lights, a man in a blazer edging toward an ancient painted coffin with a lighter, golden sand stirring

signature.title: The Weighing of the Heart
signature.place: The Crystal Street roundabout, under another sky, 3 a.m.
signature.text: The night before Halloween, the starry woman arching over Crystal Street lowers her hands, and the roundabout becomes a hall of judgment. The Heartstone tips like one pan of an enormous golden scale, and in the other pan rests a single white feather. Into the Heartstone's pan, piece by piece, float the things Glimmer Falls took and kept: a stolen stop sign, a 1911 ticket stub, a souvenir curse scroll, the gala's rubber mummy suit, and it sinks, and sinks. At the edge of the grass pads a patient creature with a crocodile's head, a lion's mane and a hippo's heavy body, waiting to see which way the scale tips. "In my country," says the queen's voice, "the dead are weighed. Tonight I weigh your town."
signature.art: A suburban roundabout at three in the morning under a vast arching figure of a woman made of stars, a glowing purple geode tilted down as one pan of an enormous golden balance scale, a single white feather resting on the other pan, a stop-shaped metal plate, a ticket stub and a rubber mummy suit floating down into the heavy pan, a creature with a crocodile's head, a lion's mane and a hippo's body pacing at the edge of the grass, a teenager stepping forward, gold and starlight, wide shot

choices.label: Step up to the scale and confess for the town: we kept what wasn't ours

success.text: You step up and say it plainly, for everybody asleep behind their doors. "We kept things that weren't ours. We kept you. We bought tickets. We're sorry, and we're going to give it back." The Heartstone's pan rises slowly until it hangs level with the feather. "A true word weighs less than a lie," says the queen. "Your town is not yet light. But it is level."
success.art: A teenager standing before an enormous golden scale on a moonlit roundabout with a hand on their heart, the glowing purple geode pan rising level with a white feather, a vast starry figure arching overhead

failure.text: Your voice cracks and you blurt that it wasn't you, you never stole anything, you weren't even born. It's true, and it weighs like a stone. The Heartstone sinks lower, and the creature pads one step closer.
failure.art: A glowing purple geode sinking low on one side of an enormous golden scale, a crocodile-headed creature stepping closer across moonlit grass, a teenager stepping back with raised hands

choices.label: Lay the true record in the pan: what was taken, from where, and by whom

success.text: A lie got her here, so you answer it with the truth: one crate, Alexandria to Minneapolis, marked MACHINE PARTS, customs waived, and under it, in your own handwriting, SHE HAS A NAME. SHE WAS STOLEN. The curse scroll and the rubber mummy suit slide off the Heartstone and blow away like old newspaper. The scale settles, level and calm.
success.art: A teenager kneeling to place a handwritten page and an old shipping document on a glowing golden scale pan, a cheap souvenir scroll and a rubber costume blowing away on the wind, the pans settling level under starlight

failure.text: You lay down what you know, and the wind takes it page by page out over the rooftops. With only the stolen things left to weigh, the scale sinks, and the stars overhead flicker like a candle about to go out.
failure.art: Loose papers whirling away over suburban rooftops under a starry sky, an enormous golden scale tipping low beneath a glowing purple geode, a teenager reaching after the pages

choices.label: Stand between the Devourer and the sleeping street

success.text: The Devourer pads up to you, crocodile jaws as long as your arm, and breathes river mud and old incense in your face. You hold out the back of your hand, the way Dr. Haddad says to greet a strange dog. It sniffs, considers, and yawns enormously. Then it lies down at your feet with a thump, chin on its paws, guarding the street beside you until the weighing is done.
success.art: A teenager holding out the back of one hand to a huge crocodile-headed lion-maned creature on a moonlit roundabout, the creature lying down with its chin on its paws, a golden scale glowing behind

failure.text: It looks at you with ancient yellow eyes and begins to slurp up your shadow from the grass, a little at a time, like spaghetti. You run. Your shadow catches up with you at home about an hour later, noticeably shorter.
failure.art: A huge crocodile-headed creature slurping up a teenager's long moonlit shadow from the grass, the teenager sprinting away down a dark suburban street, a golden scale glowing on the roundabout

finale.title: The Curse of the Pharaoh Gala
finale.place: Glimmer Falls Public Library, Halloween night
finale.text: The Halvorsen Foundation's CURSE OF THE PHARAOH Halloween Gala is in full swing: plastic palms, a fog machine, a man in a rubber mummy suit lurching around for tips. At midnight every light in the library goes out. Sand pours down the stairs like a river. The coffin lid lifts by itself, and Queen Neferet rises, not shambling, not snarling, but standing tall in white linen and gold, starlight in her eyes. The ceiling is gone and the arching sky fills the night. "I have been patient for seventy-five years," she says. "Tonight I go home, and I will take every name in this town as my fare."
finale.art: A small-town library gala in chaos on Halloween night, plastic palms and a fog machine, a man in a rubber mummy suit, golden sand pouring down the main staircase in a river, and rising from an open painted coffin a tall regal Egyptian queen with kohl-lined eyes, a white linen gown, a gold and lapis broad collar and a gold vulture crown with starlight in her eyes, the ceiling gone and a vast starry sky above, four teenagers in homemade costumes facing her, gold and blue light, wide shot

choices.label: Throw yourself on the coffin lid and force it shut

success.text: You and Wade throw your weight onto the lid as the sand roars. It bucks once, twice, then goes still. The sky folds back into an ordinary October night. By morning the Foundation has packed the crate and driven off to the next town, and nothing in Glimmer Falls is cursed. Nothing is fixed, either.
success.alone: You throw all your weight onto the lid as the sand roars. It bucks once, twice, then goes still. The sky folds back into an ordinary October night. By morning the Foundation has packed the crate and driven off to the next town, and nothing in Glimmer Falls is cursed. Nothing is fixed, either.
success.art: A teenager and a mullet-haired metalhead pressing down on a coffin lid with all their weight as swirling sand settles around them in a dark library

failure.text: The lid lifts you like a leaf. The queen regards you without anger, the way a mountain regards weather, and your own name begins to drift up out of you like a spark. You grab for it, and miss.
failure.art: A teenager lifted off their feet by a rising coffin lid, a glowing word drifting up out of their chest like a spark, a calm crowned queen watching

choices.label: Swap the shipping labels and tell her the crate is going to Egypt

success.text: You and Toby type up a perfect fake label on the AV room typewriter, LUXOR, EGYPT, URGENT, and paste it on the crate. The queen reads it, and her starlight softens. She lies down. The lid closes gently. At dawn the crate drives off toward the next tour stop in Fresno, and you feel sick about it for a long, long time.
success.alone: You type up a perfect fake label on the AV room typewriter, LUXOR, EGYPT, URGENT, and paste it on the crate. The queen reads it, and her starlight softens. She lies down. The lid closes gently. At dawn the crate drives off toward the next tour stop in Fresno, and you feel sick about it for a long, long time.
success.art: A teenager pasting a typed shipping label onto a wooden crate in a dark library, a queen lying back down in her coffin with softening starlight, a guilty-looking kid with a camcorder nearby

failure.text: She reads the label, and then she reads you. "Another lie in a box," she says. The sand stops pouring and starts rising, filling the room to your waist, your chest. "I have been lied to by greater men than you, and they are all dust now."
failure.art: Golden sand rising to a teenager's chest in a dark library, a fake shipping label floating on its surface, a queen in gold looking down with ancient disappointment

choices.label: Speak her name and show her the cartouche, the diary and the letter

success.text: You wade through the sand and say it: "Neferet, Great Royal Wife." Beside you, Mrs. Mansour speaks the old offering words, bread and beer and every good and pure thing, and the queen goes still. You hold up the cartouche, the confession in the diary and the 1972 letter. Then Gil Halvorsen pushes through the crowd, pith helmet gone, and signs a release on the back of a gala program. "She's going home," he says. "I'll pay for the flight." The queen looks at all of you for a long time. Then she smiles, and lies down to wait, for the last time, a little longer.
success.art: A crowned Egyptian queen in white linen with a gentle smile lowering herself back into her coffin as sand settles, an older woman speaking with hands raised in blessing, teens holding up a journal and a letter, a man signing a paper on a gala program

failure.text: You stumble over her name, and the gala crowd's screaming drowns out your voice. The queen hears that someone knows the truth, but not who, and not loudly enough. The sand keeps rising. You need the whole room to stop and listen.
failure.art: A teenager shouting into a panicking gala crowd in a dark library, sand rising around their legs, a queen in gold turning her head as if straining to hear

choices.label: Knock three times on the coffin, with the manners she taught you the first nights, and ask for an audience

success.text: You wade through the sand to the coffin and knock three times, slow and polite, the way a guest knocks. In the first nights of the week she spoke to you out of the dark, and she always answered good manners. She answers now. The sand stops pouring. "An audience," she says, amused, "in the middle of my own escape." With every courtesy you know, you ask her to wait one more night, not in a box this time, but as an honored guest of the library with her name on the door. She considers the plastic palms, the fog machine, the man in the rubber suit. "One night," she says. "As a guest." She lies down, and the sky folds back over Glimmer Falls as gently as a blanket.
success.art: A teenager in a Halloween costume knocking politely on an ancient painted coffin amid drifts of golden sand, a regal queen in white linen and gold rising with an amused expression, plastic palms and a fog machine behind

failure.text: You knock, but the fog machine roars and somebody shrieks "THE CURSE!" and your knock is lost in the noise. The queen doesn't hear a guest. She hears a crowd, and the sand keeps coming.
failure.art: Golden sand pouring down library stairs over panicking gala guests in costumes, a fog machine billowing, a teenager knocking on a coffin lid half buried in sand

choices.label: Storm the gala stage and shut the curse show down, the way you stood up for her that week

success.text: You've done this before. Midweek, you stood up for her in public. So you climb onto the gala stage, rip down the CURSE OF THE PHARAOH banner, yank the fog machine's plug and take the Foundation director's microphone right out of his hand. "Show's over. She isn't a curse. She's a person, and she was robbed." The man in the rubber mummy suit pulls off his head and nods. The screaming stops. In the sudden quiet the queen looks at you, and the sand stops rising. "Someone fights for me," she says, "instead of against me." She lies down to wait, and for the first time in seventy-five years she believes the waiting will end.
success.art: A teenager in a Halloween costume tearing down a gala banner on a library stage among plastic palms, a man in a rubber mummy costume pulling off his mask, a queen in white linen and gold watching with surprise

failure.text: The Foundation's security man reaches the stage first, and you go down in a heap of plastic palms. The crowd laughs, thinking it's part of the show, and the sand rises around the laughter.
failure.art: A teenager in a Halloween costume sprawled in a tangle of plastic palm trees on a library gala stage, a security guard looming, golden sand rising around laughing costumed guests

choices.label: Give back what was taken, the way you learned to the night before: her name first

success.text: The night before Halloween you learned how giving back works: you carry it yourself, and you say whose it is. So you wade through the sand and say it: "Neferet, Great Royal Wife." Beside you Mrs. Mansour speaks the old offering words, bread and beer and every good and pure thing. You hold up the cartouche, the confession in the diary and the 1972 letter, and Gil Halvorsen pushes through the crowd and signs a release on the back of a gala program. "She's going home," he says. "I'll pay for the flight." The queen takes the program in her own hands and reads her name on it, spelled right. Then she smiles, and lies down to wait, for the last time, a little longer.
success.art: A regal queen in white linen and gold holding a folded gala program, an elderly woman speaking beside her, a young man in a rumpled safari jacket holding a pen, a smiling teenager in costume, golden sand settling

failure.text: You say her name, but a Foundation lawyer is shouting about property and the crowd is shouting about curses. The queen hears that someone knows her, but not who, and not loudly enough. You need the whole room to listen.
failure.art: A teenager in a Halloween costume calling out across a crowded gala as golden sand pours down library stairs, a man in a suit shouting and waving papers, a queen in white linen listening intently

best.title: She Goes Home
best.text: In March 1987, after a winter of letters, lawyers and one very determined librarian, Queen Neferet leaves Glimmer Falls in a climate-controlled crate marked with her true name. Mrs. Mansour flies with her. Egyptian conservators meet the plane in Cairo, and in Luxor, on the west bank, families line the road and the old women say her name out loud. In the library's exhibit room a new placard reads: HERE STAYED NEFERET, GREAT ROYAL WIFE, ON HER WAY HOME. Gil Halvorsen sells the kiosk and enrolls in Egyptology. Every Halloween the stars over Crystal Street look, just for a moment, like another country's.
best.art: A small-town library exhibit room at morning, two conservators in white gloves carefully loading a padded wooden crate painted with a carved oval of hieroglyphs onto a dolly, an Egyptian American woman in her sixties resting her hand on the crate, a freckled librarian in an oxblood cardigan and three teenagers watching quietly, soft window light, medium wide shot

good.title: Next Stop, Fresno
good.text: The crate leaves town, the sand stops, and the Big Dipper comes back. Glimmer Falls forgets the whole thing by Thanksgiving. You don't. Every month you look up the Halvorsen tour schedule at the library: Fresno, Bakersfield, Reno. Somewhere out there a queen is still waiting in a box with the wrong name on it, and you can't stop thinking you could have done more.
good.art: A teenager sitting at a library table at night with a printed tour schedule spread in front of them, and through the tall window a moving truck with a wooden crate in the back pulling away under an ordinary starry sky with the Big Dipper, green lamp light, medium shot

bittersweet.title: The Wrong Name
bittersweet.text: The queen sleeps again, but the night she woke takes its toll. A few mailboxes on Crystal Street stay blank, and some neighbors never get their names quite right again: Mr. Dobbs answers to Harvey now, and he isn't sure that's wrong. The exhibit leaves. The sand in the library's book drop never quite stops, and Ms. Hart sweeps it up every morning without a word.
bittersweet.art: A freckled librarian with gray-streaked chestnut hair in an oxblood cardigan sweeping a small drift of golden sand from beneath a brass book-return slot at dawn, behind her across the street a row of mailboxes with one painted plain and bare, pale gold morning light, medium wide shot

bad.title: Unknown Teenager, 1986
bad.text: The sky closes with the queen inside it, and something else goes with her: your name. You are found on November first in her empty glass case, breathing slow and deep like a sleeper who cannot be woken, and nobody, not your crew, not your family, can remember what to call you. The Foundation adds you to the tour. Your placard reads UNKNOWN TEENAGER, PROVENANCE SUBURBAN CALIFORNIA. Far away, a queen is finally home, and she is sorry about the fare.
bad.art: A teenager asleep in a museum glass case with folded hands and slow breath fogging the glass, three worried friends pressing their palms against the outside of the case, a tour group in the background, white display light, medium shot
